articles.title: NHL 27 Is Using AI-Generated Voiceover for In-Game Commentators, John Buccigross Says
articles.summary: EA Sports is using generative AI to create voiceover for its in-game commentators in NHL 27, according to veteran sports commentator John Buccigross.
articles.body:
EA Sports is using generative AI to create voiceover for its in-game commentators in NHL 27 , according to veteran sports commentator John Buccigross.

When speaking on the Chirping Zebras podcast (initially spotted by Insider Gaming's Mike Straw ), Buccigross was talking about his experience working with EA Sports on the NHL games. He revealed that he will be in NHL 27, but EA also used generative AI to add voice lines as well.

"They're using some AI now; they played me some stuff back of my voice," said Buccigross. "It's like 'Wow, that's pretty good!' If that means less work but the same check, I'll take it. Sometimes AI will get something wrong. One of the guys was playing it back, and a lot of these guys maybe aren't hardcore sports fans; they're video game extrordinares. They're not always up on the vernacular. So they're playing back my AI voice, and they're like, 'Score! And the crowd gets out of their chairs!' I was like, 'No, they're not chairs. They look like chairs, but we call them seats.'

"So, little things like that, you gotta go back and listen because words matter. [...] But then you can make AI smarter; in the future they'll say seats, they won't say chairs. You have to manually put that in. That was kind of a funny anecdote from the process."

Generative AI is becoming increasingly common in the gaming industry, despite some fans pushing back on it. Call of Duty faced backlash for using AI to generate cosmetic items such as calling cards last year, and now, EA Sports seems to be embracing it in many of its games this year. This year's installments of College Football, Madden, and FC all have labels on their respective Steam pages that notify players of the use of generative AI in development. NHL is not on Steam, so there's no such disclaimer.

IGN has reached out to EA for comment on how AI is being used in the case of NHL 27 and if it extends beyond the game's voiceover content. NHL 27 launches for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S September 11, 2026. IGN reviewed the game and gave it a 6/10 , noting that, although it's fun, it doesn't do much to improve upon its predecessor.

"Hockey is one of the greatest sports in the world, and NHL 27 remains enjoyable largely due to that simple fact," reads an excerpt from the review. "The satisfaction of delivering a bone-crushing hit or snapping a wrist shot past a goaltender is just as effective as ever, and tiny tweaks to stuff like stadiums and music continue to add authenticity in small doses – but there are no illusions that anything truly substantial has changed this year."

articles.title: Levelling Up with LG: How 5K is Changing the Gaming Monitor in 2026
articles.summary: Levelling Up with LG: How 5K is Changing the Gaming Monitor in 2026
articles.body:
At the heart of any PC setup is your monitor. You can have the fastest and most powerful rig and peripherals going around, but it’s all bottlenecked by how fast and detailed you can see it.

LG has long been one of the leaders in the space, and the tech giant has just launched two new models that have caught our eye.

For those tight for space, the 27” LG UltraGear evo GM9 (27GM950B) Hyper Mini LED 5K monitor. And for gamers with a more spacious setup, the ultrawide OLED experience offered by the 39” LG UltraGear evo GX9 (39GX950B).

These are the next evolutionary step for the LG range, a foray into the territory of 5K content driven by an industry-first feature – AI upscaling to 5K in a gaming monitor. Game experiences outputted at WFHD (2560×1080) or higher resolution, are upscaled - on device! – up to 5K (depending on input quality), providing huge benefits to gamers.

Why? You don’t have to level-up your rig to get the result. As the 5K upscaling is done on the monitor, your existing PC hardware isn’t put under any additional strain, and you may not have to upgrade your desktop to benefit.

Breaking down the 27” LG UltraGear evo GM9

You’ll struggle to find a 27” monitor as sharp as the LG UltraGear evo GM9. Its 5120x2880 resolution presents over 14-million pixels at 218PPI, which doesn’t just make text far easier to read, but brings details like an opponent’s weapon into clarity.

The Hyper Mini LED panel also plays a key role. The “hyper” referring to the improvements in dimming zones (2,304) and LEDs (9,216) over a traditional Mini LED monitor (1.5x and 5.9x respectively). It allows the monitor to hit a peak brightness of 1250 nits and achieve both HDR 1000 while dramatically reducing blooming. All with Mini LED durability!

Sick of not seeing a muzzle-flash? Missing enemies hiding in the shadows? Is your target blurring as it runs across the screen? Not with the GM9.

It’s rich with other gaming features, too, including a 1ms grey-to-grey response time and VRR (NVIDIA G-SYNC, AMD FreeSync Premium). But Dual Mode has the most dynamic impact. At 5K, the monitor can refresh 165 times a second, accepting a very solid frame rate in full detail. But if you’re happy to sacrifice resolution for speed, Dual Mode doubles the Hz while reducing the resolution, happily receiving 330fps at 1440p.

It’s all unlocked by Ultra‑High Bit Rate 20 (UHBR20) support via the DisplayPort 2.1 port. It’s the highest bandwidth mode available in 2026, allowing that great resolution, refresh rate and HDR to journey from your GPU to the monitor.

That’s excellent. You can still immerse in 5K cinematic gaming experiences, then activate Dual Mode when speed-of-play is key – like multiplayer or racing games.

Breaking down the 39” LG UltraGear evo GX9

If you’ve never gamed on an ultrawide curved monitor before… oh boy. It takes immersion to a new level as the game world bleeds into your periphery. It feels like you’re really racing that car. Really standing on the bridge of that ship. Really climbing that ancient ruin. Plus, it’s awesome for productivity, too – like having two desktops in one.

Historically, ultrawide means sacrificing resolution, but the GX9 doesn’t compromise with its 5120x2160 (5K2K) resolution at 143ppi. The contrast in these panels is insanity at 1.85M:1, hitting a peak brightness of 1500 nits and HDR True Black 500. All leaning into the benefits of OLED, with a 0.03ms grey-to-grey response time.

The space between black and light is so distinct it pops – Cyberpunk 2077, Alan Wake, Hellblade and the like find new life. And like the GM9, it can keep pace with even the most powerful rigs, delivering 165Hz at 5K2K, or 330Hz at WFHD via Dual Mode. All while stuttering and tearing is fragged by the VRR power of NVIDIA G-SYNC and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro.

In gaming, now remains then… but with these new LG monitors, the gap is closing. These specs aren’t window dressing. They work together in a meaningful way to ensure you can finally see what your PC is delivering, meaning you can react faster. For gaming that means more immersion, better performance and more victories. While for your work productivity, you get to benefit from crisp clarity, more realistic colours and deeper contrast, reducing eye fatigue and improving precision.

articles.title: First Xiaomi, then the world: why Arm might give phone gaming a huge graphics boost
articles.summary: After five years of development, Arm now has a dedicated AI gaming graphics accelerator inside its GPU, the Arm Mali G2-Ultra NX.
articles.body: China is getting first crack at a British technology that might change how mobile games are made and played. Today, the Xiaomi 18 Fold launches in mainland China with an Arm Mali G2-Ultra NX graphics processor inside its custom Xring O3 chip. What’s so special about that? After five years of development, Arm now has an AI gaming graphics accelerator inside its GPU. By following Nvidia’s playbook, Arm-powered phones are about to have PC-like technologies to make games run faster, at higher resolution, with advanced lighting techniques, all without using more power than they do today. The jagged edges you see in the mobile versions of popular games might begin to go away. And these advancements won’t just be locked to Chinese phones. The chips, devices, and games are already inbound. “You will be able to buy it; you will be able to get it in phones next year, you will be able to get it in other types of larger screen devices, whether that be tablets or Chromebooks,” Arm’s Chris Bergey, EVP of Edge AI, tells The Verge in an interview. While he can’t say which other devices will contain the Mali G2-Ultra NX, he hints that some of Google’s upcoming Googlebooks might use this graphics tech as well. “We think it’s going to be huge,” Bergey tells me. DLSS for Android There are two ways to look at Arm’s new Arm Mali G2-Ultra NX. One is that it’s stronger than prior mobile GPUs, period, with an alleged 85-percent performance increase over the GPU that Xiaomi was using previously, and a 14 percent increase over Arm’s previous flagship in “non-AI gaming.” But the other, more important way is that it enables a suite of hardware-accelerated graphical techniques that sound very similar to Nvidia’s DLSS, including AI upscaling (where it imagines a higher-resolution image), frame generation (where it generates new “fake” frames between existing ones), and even ray reconstruction like Nvidia’s DLSS 4.5. [Image: “This really is about bringing Tensor-like capabilities into the GPU shader,” Bergey tells us. Arm is calling all of these techniques “neural graphics,” but it doesn’t mean quite the same thing as when Nvidia uses that term — we’re not talking about enhancing faces by reimagining how light and shadow work, at least not just yet. [Image: Note: Games won’t necessarily feel four times faster even if they look that way. Instead, these improvements are about speed, offering what Arm claims is up to four times the framerate when “Neural Super Sampling,” “Neural Frame Rate Upscaling” and “Neural Denoising” are all applied simultaneously, because each technique lets the system do less work rendering actual pixels and frames, counting on AI to fill in the rest. [Media: Note that games likely won’t feel four times faster, though, even if they look that way. Half of the boost is because your phone will imagine new frames between existing ones — and when Nvidia, AMD, and Intel do “frame generation,” it typically comes with the cost of additional latency. Regardless, these techniques won’t all arrive immediately. “The first titles will largely be super sampling,” says Bergey, with frame gen coming in early 2027 and denoising “soon after that.” But when you put them together, he says a phone can now genuinely play an experience like this Neural Dawn technology demo, below — and without draining your battery fast. “It might be like, hey, you can now play 1080p, 60 frames per second for three hours,” Bergey tells me. “In the past, it was 30 minutes.” [Media: With the Xiaomi Pad 9 Pro Max tablet, which pairs Arm’s GPU with a larger battery, screen, and surface area for cooling, may offer even more performance. The Chinese company is showing off 3.2K resolution at 120 frames per second. Bergey says that an entire phone with these chips will consume no more than 2.5 watts, with only 1.5 watts allotted to the GPU. “That’s basically what you want for real sustained gaming where it’s not getting warm in your phone, you’re not like ‘Oh, where’s my charger,’ that kind of thing,” says Bergey. Or, he says, device and chipset makers can run this GPU at lower wattage to last longer. It’s not just for gaming phones: “This is not overclocking, this is mainstream,” he says. “This is about AI replacing traditional rendering; anywhere you can use it, you will use it,” he says. [Image: Xiaomi claims its flagship Xiaomi Pad 9 Pro Max tablet, with the same Xring O3 chip, can play games at 3.2K resolution and 120fps. It’s not just for premium phones and tablets, either: “While Mali G2-Ultra NX targets flagship smartphones, neural graphics will also be available across the Premium and Pro configurations, bringing the technology to a broader range of mobile segments and tiers.” Arm isn’t the only one attempting to push these speed-boosting PC technologies into the mobile realm. The developers of the graphically intensive Stellar Blade, for example, recently revealed they’re making their game run at 60fps on the Nintendo Switch 2 by using both Nvidia’s DLSS and a version of AMD’s frame generation technique. The Switch 2 has an Arm-based mobile chip too, though it contains a custom Nvidia GPU. Like with the most advanced versions of Nvidia, AMD, and Intel’s techniques, game developers will need to integrate Arm’s features into their games, though participating game engines like Unreal Engine and Unity can help. Bergey doesn’t think it’s a switch gamers will be able to flip for just any game they like. [Image: Arm’s partners. Where Winds Meet, Infinity Nikki and Arena Breakout: Infinite are the first three games confirmed to take advantage of Arm’s new graphics accelerator, and Bergey tells us more games are on the way. Some will be announced in the coming weeks, he says — he’s just not allowed to reveal them quite yet.

articles.title: Nintendo Store Leak Reveals The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Switch 2 Remake Pricing
articles.summary: It looks like Nintendo has inadvertently revealed how much its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will cost on Switch 2.
articles.body:
It looks like Nintendo has inadvertently revealed how much its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will cost on Switch 2.

Ahead of today's dedicated Legend of Zelda Nintendo Direct broadcast, Ocarina of Time's digital edition appeared on the Australian Nintendo Store, priced at AUD $94.95 (thanks, Vooks ). The listing is now offline.

How does this compare to other Switch 2 games? Well, this is the same Australian price point as Yoshi and the Mysterious Book, which costs $59.99 in the U.S. or £49.99 in the U.K. In other words, this is the cheaper Switch 2 price point, rather than the premium $69.99 cost charged for Mario Kart World or Donkey Kong Bananza.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Trailer June 2026 Nintendo Direct - Screenshots

Remember, of course, that Nintendo now employs a range of prices for its Switch 2 games (this year's Star Fox was cheaper still, at $49.99). Newer Switch 2 games also now typically cost more for a physical copy, with the digital download version less expensive.

What does this mean for the Ocarina of Time remake itself? Well, it's hard to say — though naturally this suggests the game will not be presented in the same way as an all-new title akin to Breath of the Wild or Tears of the Kingdom. Both of those cost $79.99 for their Nintendo Switch 2 versions.

Stay with us on IGN throughout today as we discover much, much more of Nintendo's plans for The Legend of Zelda, including Ocarina of Time and (hopefully!) a first trailer for the live-action movie. As ever, we'll be reporting live.

articles.title: Andrew Garfield Says He Hopes Billionaires Are 'Scared S**tless' by His New Movie, The Uprising
articles.summary: Andrew Garfield has said he hopes that any billionaires who see his new movie, The Uprising, are “scared s**tless” by it.
articles.body:
Andrew Garfield has said he hopes that any billionaires who see his new movie, The Uprising , are “scared s**tless” by it.

The former Spider-Man actor spoke about The Uprising as part of a Q&A alongside director Paul Greengrass ahead of the movie’s launch this week. The Uprising depicts the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, which was fueled by King Richard II’s brutal tax on the poorest members of English society. Garfield plays Ploughman, a farmer who leads the rebellion. Some of the marketing has suggested it’s a Robin Hood origin story . The Uprising is even a game within Fortnite .

In the Q&A, Greengrass and Garfield said that The Uprising is an immediately relevant story, despite it being set 700 years ago. And Garfield specifically singled out today’s billionaires, saying The Uprising should act as a cautionary tale.

“I hope it's galvanizing,” Garfield said of The Uprising. “I hope there's some awakening that people feel, that we all feel like our own struggles are being reflected in the struggles of these characters from a distant time and place, and that it could be directive.

“And I hope that if any billionaires watch it, that they're scared s***less.”

There’s a long list of billionaires Garfield could be referencing here, but it’s easy to imagine his comment referring to everyone from X / Twitter owner Elon Musk to Amazon owner Jeff Bezos. And at a time when the desperation to win the AI arms race has thrown caution — and, some say, our humanity — to the wind, there is growing concern that mass job losses and societal upheaval caused by our relentless pursuit of AI may cause civil unrest .

The Most Famous Movie and TV Characters Who've Met Robin Hood

The Uprising’s tagline is “there will be no peace until we are healed,” and Garfield passed the sentiment on to the aforementioned billionaires.

“I'm going to include the billionaires in that as well cuz they're the ones that might be the most soul sick,” he declared. “They're the ones that might need the healing the most in a way.”

While we wait for a fresh uprising, Garfield might find the time to watch Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey. He recently admitted he hadn’t yet congratulated his Spider-Man co-star Tom Holland on the incredible success of both movies because he hadn’t seen them.

articles.title: The War for Westeros Developers Are Planning for a Flood of Game of Thrones Fans Who Have Never Played an RTS
articles.summary: War for Westeros is a real-time strategy game for real-time strategy enthusiasts, but the developers at PlaySide know they’re going to get inundated with Game of Thrones fans who have never played an RTS before when the game comes out — so they’re planning accordingly.
articles.body:
War for Westeros is a real-time strategy game for real-time strategy enthusiasts, but the developers at PlaySide know they’re going to get inundated with Game of Thrones fans who have never played an RTS before when the game comes out — so they’re planning accordingly.

The Game of Thrones franchise is, as everyone knows, incredibly popular, and that popularity is maintained by spinoff HBO shows such as House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms years after Game of Thrones itself came to an end. And so, War for Westeros will surely find itself beset by players from two camps: RTS fans who are looking for their next strategy hit, and Game of Thrones fans who fancy playing a game set in Westeros.

RTS games, though, can be pretty complex and hard to get into. RTS developers have for years tried to solve this problem with various systems and tutorials. War for Westeros will, obviously, have tutorials to help newcomers learn its systems, but PlaySide has built approachability into the very design of the game to help.

Game of Thrones: War for Westeros Screenshots

“That's what we want!” game director Ryan McMahon told me in an interview at gamescom, when I asked if the studio was prepared for the flood or RTS-shy Game of Thrones fans to descend upon War for Westeros.

“Approachable is the key word,” he continued. “So you've got accessibility and approachability. We kind of look at it more through the approachability lens. It's not trying to dumb down what makes a good RTS, but more so how we onboard players to that experience.”

So, expect a “very robust” tutorial at launch to onboard new players to skirmish mode and teach players its various systems through campaign mode. But most interesting to me is that War for Westeros’s worker units do not require any high level micro mastery. In many RTS games, you need to assign workers to farm resources and construct buildings, then, once they’re done, you need to give them another job to do. And another. And another. In short, workers require constant attention.

War for Westeros, however, employs a ‘set and forget’ system where buildings will farm resources on their own once they’re build, leaving you free to focus on other things, like killing super powerful dragons.

“At the base top level of the game, there's no high level micro mastery required of your workers or your builders,” McMahon explained. “All they need to do is build a building and it's ‘set and forget.’ You don't have to assign workers to buildings to farm resources. The buildings will farm the resources on their own once they're built. So that reduces a lot of macro or mental overload of what you're trying to think about while you play the game, and allows you to focus more on the units you're building, the heroes you're fielding, what type of buildings you're placing, and creating the moments that you want to see.”

Meanwhile, the AI is tuned to give players the breathing room to learn how War for Westeros works through single-player in the hope that they’ll come away considering giving multiplayer a chance. “If they ever want to dip their toes into multiplayer or play with their friends, there's enough layers of complexity that they've been onboarded to over time without having to master straight away to enjoy a game,” McMahon said.

Certainly, War for Westeros will have plenty that is familiar for Game of Thrones fans. It has iconic characters complete with their likenesses from the HBO show — although soundalike voice actors were employed for dialogue ("Obviously choosing the actual actors would be a very expensive endeavor and also some of them aren't necessarily available to work with us on the timelines that we have"). Jon Snow, with his likeness approved by actor Kit Harington, is just one example. At gamescom, PlaySide announced Gregor ‘The Mountain’ Clegane and Arya Stark. The Mountain can be recruited by House Lannister, “utilising his massive size and strength to shock battlelines and strike fear into the hearts of those who stand against him.” Arya, on the other hand, “is a master assassin for House Stark, trained under the Faceless Men of the House of Black and White.”

I had suspected that Jon Snow would be the most popular pick in playtests because, well, it’s Jon Snow. But according to McMahon, as the game has evolved and staff have got to grips with it, other famous characters have risen to the top of the popularity tree — and with good reason.

“Tywin [Lannister] and Robb [Stark] are actually the most popular,” McMahon revealed. “The cavalry definitely helps so they can get around the map really quickly. But they have a strong kit in how they buff units around them as commanders, which helps reinforce the army rather than being individual strength.

“But it changes a lot. We do weekly play tests every Friday afternoon after lunch, we just play the game for the rest of the day. And at the end of every milestone we do an internal tournament as well where we basically play whatever the game is currently at, and we have a bracket system and whoever wins gets the trophy and that gets passed around desk to desk based on who won the last tournament.

“So we get a lot of data from that because we've got data in the game that we're tracking and we can see win rates from different factions. We can see how many heroes get spawned. We get a heat map of where people build buildings on the map that informs our level design and informs our faction balance and informs how we basically gear up heroes in different factions against each other.”

Currently, players are picking heroes based on what they believe will be most effective on the battlefield as opposed to going with their heart and their favorite character. That makes a lot of sense if you're running internal tournaments.

“As the game gets more mature, it sort of moved that way,” McMahon said. “For a while it was Jon [Snow] and Jaime [Lannister] because they were very strong heroes. But now if we put more emphasis on the units being important, because the game needs to be grounded. You can't just have one hero fighting off hundreds of people. Commanders start to become more important because they're not that strong on their own, but they're also reinforcing the units they're paired with.”

I suspect when War for Westeros comes out on PC next year, Jon Snow might rise to the top once again.

articles.title: Call of Duty 2 Signaled the Beginning of the End of Halo's Reign as the King of Console Shooters
articles.summary: Call of Duty 2 was, quite simply, the right game at the right time for Xbox 360. It showed gamers what the new console was capable of while also being a stellar game regardless of platform. It probably wouldn't hold up today, honestly, but if you had the pleasure of being there at the time, it was a heck of a moment in the history of Xbox.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Ryan McCaffrey, who worked at Official Xbox Magazine from 2002-2012 during the original Xbox and Xbox 360 era before joining IGN, where he remains “the Xbox guy.” In the run-up to Xbox’s 25th anniversary, he’ll be sharing his memories from the platform’s first quarter-century.

Younger readers might not remember a time when Call of Duty wasn't one of the biggest franchises in all of gaming, but I promise you that there was a time. I had played the original on PC — the only platform it had been released on — back in 2003. And, yes, I quite liked it. It was an excellent World War 2-set military first-person shooter.

When it came time for the sequel in 2005, which was slated to be a day-one launch title for the then-upcoming Xbox 360 console, my Official Xbox Magazine colleagues and I were excited about it, but it wasn't necessarily the most anticipated Xbox 360 launch game. (In hindsight, nothing really was; while the original Xbox had a killer app in Halo: Combat Evolved, it had little else in its launch lineup, whereas the Xbox 360 had a few excellent games — like Project Gotham Racing 3, Condemned: Criminal Origins, and of course Call of Duty 2 — but no Halo-level must-haves.)

My eager but not feverish anticipation for Call of Duty 2 changed when I got to go to Infinity Ward in the summer of 2005 to do a cover story on Infinity Ward's sequel. And I remember very clearly what jumped out at my first as I was shown an early mission from the campaign: the volumetric smoke effects. With the increased horsepower of the Xbox 360, smoke grenades mattered more than ever during gameplay, as tossing them to obscure the enemy's vision while you darted across the path nearby Axis a-holes was integrated into the mission design.

It was a really fun way to work the Xbox 360's new tricks into the action. Couple that with the excellent sound effects and surround-sound audio work the Xbox had baked in (in fairness, the original Xbox was also fully 5.1-capable) and I suddenly found myself looking forward to Call of Duty 2 more than any other game in the 360's rather large launch lineup.

Fast-forward to the fall of that year and the imminent launch of the new Xbox. As I've mentioned before in some of my other Xbox 25th anniversary look-backs at my favorite games from the platform's past, magazines are made well in advance in order to allow time for printing and shipping to our hundreds of thousands of subscribers. This meant that we typically got access to review builds of games well in advance (think: two months). This was usually no problem for developers to provide, as the submission builds they'd submit to the Xbox certification team were typically pretty final; the age of day-one patches had not yet dawned.

But in this case, I had to go to the game, rather than the other way around, as security was tight around both the new Xbox and the new Call of Duty. And so I returned to Infinity Ward in southern California to spend a few days reviewing Call of Duty 2. I began with campaign before moving to multiplayer (against the Infinity Ward QA testers and multiplayer team, who had the distinct advantage of having played dozens if not hundreds of hours of multiplayer compared to my zero hours). Remember earlier when I said I quite enjoyed the original Call of Duty on PC? Call of Duty 2's campaign on Xbox 360 was significantly better. More action, more drama, more tension. It was wildly impressive by any metric, which was especially important considering that Call of Duty multiplayer had not yet established itself as the main reason many people bought each new game.

Make no mistake, though: multiplayer was awesome. Multiple game modes, a short TTK (remember, it was all pretty new at the time!), killer graphics, and don't forget it was the pre-Party Chat era when most people actually used the Chat Headset bundled with every Xbox 360 and communicated with their teammates. Looking back, it was the beginning of the end of Halo's reign as the king of console shooters. Halo 2 was absolutely still being played by a ton of people after the Xbox 360 launched (as you may recall, Halo 1 and 2 were the first two backwards compatible games with Xbox 360, and that compatibility was baked into the new console out of the box), and Halo 3 would have its moment two years later...right before Infinity Ward's next project, Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, took the crown from Halo for good.

Call of Duty 2 was, quite simply, the right game at the right time for Xbox 360. It showed gamers what the new console was capable of while also being a stellar game regardless of platform. It probably wouldn't hold up today, honestly, but if you had the pleasure of being there at the time, it was a heck of a moment in the history of Xbox.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Is Up for Preorder
articles.summary: Preorders are live for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake for Nintendo Switch 2 – and once again, physical copies cost $10 more than digital.
articles.body:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake is set to release exclusively for Nintendo Switch 2 on November 5. A from-the-ground-up remake of one of the most beloved video games of all time, it features improved visuals and playability both on the TV and on the go. It’s available now for preorder ( see it at Nintendo ).

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (Switch 2)

As is Nintendo's custom this console generation , there’s a $10 price difference between physical and digital copies of the game, with physical copies being more expensive. The MSRP for the game is $59.99 for digital copies and $69.99 for physical copies. For what it's worth, for physical copies, the full game comes on the cartridge .

For other recent Switch 2 exclusive, including Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave and Switch Sports Resort, both Amazon and Walmart have cut $10 off the price of the physical version ahead of launch. Then, once the game is out, the price goes back up. Either or both retailers may end up tweaking their prices before the game comes out.

What Is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake?

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake is a full remake of the 1998 Nintendo 64 original game.

This isn’t the first time Ocarina has been remade. A 3D version of the game was released for Nintendo 3DS in 2011. It had improved graphics and a number of quality of life improvements over the original. The original N64 version of Ocarina of Time is also available on Nintendo Switch Online Expansion Pack.

There have also been a couple of Legend of Zelda LEGO sets , including The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time - The Final Battle , which actually contains spoilers for the end of this game, so tread carefully if you haven’t played it yet.

The first footage shows that Dexter's age is catching up to him as he needs to buy some glasses for the first time, but of course, that hasn't stopped him from slaying other killers. We see a few quick cuts of Dexter's deadly routine, but it doesn't reveal much beyond what you might expect.

He's back and sharper than ever 🔪 #DexterResurrection Season 2 premieres October 30th on the #ParamountPlus Premium Plan. pic.twitter.com/oOYKWDTZCo — Dexter (@SHO_Dexter) September 8, 2026

He's back and sharper than ever 🔪 #DexterResurrection Season 2 premieres October 30th on the #ParamountPlus Premium Plan. pic.twitter.com/oOYKWDTZCo

However, Entertainment Weekly has a preview of Season 2 which reveals more details. The new season will feature a three-year time jump, allowing for Dexter's son, Harrison, to age up and become a cop. His son is now 21 and working with the NYPD, which is bound to create some kind of conflict for the pair. Dexter himself is dealing with a mid-life crisis, which manifests itself through two main antagonists: one who is much older and one who is much younger.

The younger of the two is Lucas Stark AKA the Five Borough Killer, who is stealing Dexter's thunder in New York City, according to showrunner Clyde Phillips.

“He is killing in each borough to terrorize the city,” said Phillips when speaking to EW. “In his own weird midlife crisis way, one of the things that Dexter has always wanted is recognition. At the end of Season 1 of the original series, we have the scene where he’s being feted with confetti and people cheering him on and an airplane goes by with ‘I heart Dexter.’ As independent as he likes to think he is, he wants that recognition, and by the time the Five Borough Killer has killed one person, he already has the city in his grip. And that drives Dexter f***ing crazy, because nobody knows who he is.”

As for the older killer, Brian Cox will play the New York Ripper , an aging and brutal killer who terrorizes the families of his former victims. The character was teased in Season 1 when Dexter and Harrison saw pictures of one of the Ripper's victims, as well as a recording of one of his disturbing phone calls.

“First of all, who would not want to work with Brian Cox? He is the master of the masterclass. Always prepared, always powerful,” Phillips said. “The word that I’ve been using is gravitas. You believe that this guy could do the horrible things he’s done. We meet him and he’s in a wheelchair, but he still terrorizes the survivors of the people he killed in phone calls. With a voice modulator, he’ll say, ‘Today would’ve been Rachel’s 40th birthday, you must miss her.’”

The new season of Dexter is jam-packed with stars such as Gabriel Luna, Brian Cox, Dan Stevens, Kane Hodder , and even Chris Jericho . The likes of Uma Thurman and Krysten Ritter will also return , alongside some more spoiler-y faces from Dexter's past . It's sure to be another blood-filled thrill ride.

articles.title: Godzilla Minus Zero Trailer Confirms King Ghidorah
articles.summary: The first full trailer for Godzilla Minus Zero has confirmed the sequel will feature King Ghidorah.
articles.body:
The first full trailer for Godzilla Minus Zero has confirmed the sequel will feature King Ghidorah.

Toho's minute-and-a-half trailer starts off as many may have expected. It's carnage for familiar characters like Ryunosuke Kamiki's Kôichi Shikishima and Minami Hamabe's Noriko Ôishi as what seems to be Godzilla has returned, but then we hear the familiar screech of the King of the Monsters' most iconic foe.

"Don't worry," one character in the Godzilla Minus Zero trailer can be heard saying as Ghidorah's call creeps in, "this isn't Godzilla we're talking about."

Everything ends here. Experience GODZILLA MINUS ZERO, the first-ever Japanese production #FilmedForIMAX , in theatres November 6. pic.twitter.com/S2m1hwZYdl — GODZILLA.OFFICIAL (@Godzilla_Toho) September 8, 2026

Everything ends here. Experience GODZILLA MINUS ZERO, the first-ever Japanese production #FilmedForIMAX , in theatres November 6. pic.twitter.com/S2m1hwZYdl

"War reduced Japan to zero, and Godzilla plunged it into minus," an official description said. "Two years have passed since then, and the country has faced agonizing struggles to achieve recovery and finally reclaim its daily life. Just as humanity managed to cling to a hard-won peace, a new threat strikes, crushing hope in an instant. There is no third time. Everything ends here."

Fans have long speculated that Toho's Godzilla Minus One sequel would introduce a second kaiju for Godzilla to face off against, but theories have failed to center on one creature. One of the funnier theories, for example, saw viewers (mostly jokingly) speculating that an Anguirus variant they dubbed "Gravity Anguirus" would be the one responsible for some of the floating debris shown in previous teasers.

Alas, Gravity Anguirus will not be fighting this more brutal take on Godzilla, but King Ghidorah should suffice. In hindsight, Ghidorah's "Monster Zero" alias does line up with the film's title.

The three-headed, lightning-breathing monster unfortunately doesn't make a proper appearance in the Godzilla Minus Zero trailer, but the sound of Ghidorah's roar is unmistakable. There's also the fact that we see a shot of what seems to be a yellow scale, as well as a glimpse of Godzilla falling from the sky, teasing the idea that we're in for an all-out kaiju brawl this November.

Godzilla Minus Zero is scheduled to drop into theaters November 6, 2026, meaning there isn't much time for Toho to reveal what its new Ghidorah will look like – if it doesn't plan on saving the reveal for theaters, of course. There's more than the introduction of another monster backing the Godzilla sequel as an especially important release, though.

As noted multiple times in the trailer, Godzilla Minus Zero is the first Japanese production filmed for Imax after Minus One premiered to critical and commercial success on its legendarily low budget back in 2023. The sequel was once again handled by writer, director, and VFX supervisor Takashi Yamazaki , but judging by the mentions of there being "no third time," it doesn't seem as though there will ever be a third movie.

For now, it's unclear how exactly King Ghidorah and Godzilla will meet. While we wait for Godzilla Minus Zero to arrive, you can check out IGN's 8/10 review . "A grand, sweeping blockbuster, Godzilla Minus One is light on terror and heavy on spectacle," we said at the time.
